summary: This unit teaches you to give a safe acrylic nail service: consult with the client and check for contraindications, set up a ventilated and hygienic nail desk, prepare the natural nail, apply acrylic over tips or sculpt it on forms, finish and check the nails, give aftercare advice, and carry out infills and safe removal. Safe handling of monomer, primer, dust and acetone runs through every step.

blocks.p: Acrylic nail enhancement is a service in which you build a hard, shaped layer of acrylic on the client's own nail, either to strengthen it or to add length. It is for GENERAL BEAUTY THERAPY LEVEL 2 trainees. It brings together the skills you already have (consultation, hygiene, hand and nail care) with new ones: handling strong chemicals, controlling vapour and dust, and shaping a product that sets in a few minutes.

A well-made set looks natural, feels light and lasts for weeks. A badly made set can lift, trap germs, cause an allergy for life, or tear the natural nail. That is why this unit is about **safety, preparation and control** as much as the finished look.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and practical tasks in the Centre's salon, done in a group where each member is both technician and client. The assessor watches your consultation, safety, preparation, application and clean-down, not only the finished nails.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In practical work, photograph only the hands and nails and the work area. Never photograph a client's or partner's face. If a partner has a contraindication or does not agree to be a client, work on a practice hand instead.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Working safely with chemicals, vapour and dust

blocks.p: Acrylic work uses liquids that give off vapour, filing makes fine dust, and several products can burn skin or catch fire. You will breathe this air for many hours a week, so the habits in this section protect your own health as much as your client's.

blocks.h: The hazards at the nail desk

head: Hazard
Risk
How you control it
rows: Monomer vapour
Headache, dizziness, sore eyes, nose and throat; breathing problems with long exposure
Extraction at the desk that draws vapour away from both of you
A well-ventilated room
Small, covered dappen dish; bottles closed straight after use
Filing dust
Irritates the eyes, nose, throat and skin; dust carries cured and uncured product
Extraction switched on while you file
Dust mask and safety glasses
Brush dust into the extractor or wipe it up; never blow it away
Liquid and powder on the skin
Irritation and allergic reaction (sensitisation), which can last for life
Keep product off your own and the client's skin
Nitrile gloves, changed once they are soiled
Leave a small gap at the cuticle and side walls
Acid primer
Corrosive: it can burn skin and eyes
Apply sparingly to the natural nail plate only
Close the bottle at once
Keep it off skin and out of reach of children
Fire
Monomer, primer, acetone and cleansers are flammable
No smoking, naked flames, candles, mosquito coils or heat near the desk
Small amounts only; lidded metal waste bin
Acetone
Dries skin; strong vapour; flammable
Skin protected with oil or barrier cream; ventilated area; keep from heat
Files, tip cutters and electrical equipment
Cuts, scratches, shock, overheating
Check cables and plugs; keep leads clear of walkways
Report damaged equipment and do not use it
Posture at the desk
Back, neck and wrist strain
Good light, a chair at the right height and breaks to stretch your hands

blocks.note: A paper dust mask traps dust but **not vapour**. Switch on the extraction even when you wear a mask. Never rely on a fan that blows air across the desk: it pushes vapour towards the client's face and yours. A room with the doors and windows kept shut makes the vapour worse, not better.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Use desk extraction (a small fan unit that pulls air down and away from the nails, through a filter) and also let fresh air in through a window or louvres.
Air-conditioned rooms with all windows sealed recirculate the same air: add extraction that vents outside, or one with filters the maker says suit nail products.
Air freshener only covers smell. It does not remove vapour or dust.
Replace or clean extractor filters as the maker says, or the unit stops working.

blocks.note: Jamaica's power supply is 110 V (and 220 V for some heavy equipment) at 50 Hz. Check that an extractor or lamp is made for the socket it is plugged into, and never run a cable across a wet floor. During a power cut the extraction stops: close the bottles and the dish, and do not carry on with liquid monomer until the power is back.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: **Nitrile gloves** are usually best for monomer: latex and thin vinyl are less resistant and latex can cause allergy. Change them when soiled and wash your hands before you put on a new pair.
Gloves are for handling liquids, wiping and clean-up. For filing, wear a **dust mask** and **safety glasses**.
Do not eat, drink or smoke at the desk. Wash your hands before you eat.
Long hair tied back; no loose jewellery that could dip into product.

blocks.h: Why MMA must never be used

blocks.p: **MMA** (methyl methacrylate) is a cheap liquid that makes a very hard, strongly bonded enhancement. It is not safe for nails and many countries have banned or warned against it in nail products. Professional liquid is **EMA** (ethyl methacrylate). Never use MMA.

head: Why MMA is dangerous
What it means for the client
rows: It bonds so hard that it will not break away from the nail
A knock tears the natural nail plate off the nail bed instead of the product cracking
It is very hard to soak off
Technicians over-file the natural nail to get it off; the nail ends up thin and sore
It can cause strong skin and nail allergy
Itching, redness, swelling, and loss of the nail in the worst cases
It has a very sharp, strong smell and irritating vapour
Headaches, breathing problems

ul: Buy liquid only in a **labelled** bottle that states what it is and comes with a **safety data sheet** (SDS).
Be suspicious of very cheap liquid, unlabelled bottles or a liquid that smells much stronger than EMA. Refuse it, and tell your supervisor.

blocks.p: The maker's **safety data sheet** lists a product's hazards, first aid, safe handling, storage, fire-fighting and disposal. Read it before you use a new product, keep a copy in the salon where staff can find it, and follow it together with the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules.

blocks.h: First aid at the nail desk

head: What happened
What you do
rows: Monomer on the skin
Wipe it off at once, then wash with soap and water. Do not let it dry on the skin.
Primer or monomer in the eye

Rinse the eye straight away with plenty of clean running water for several minutes, with the head tilted so water runs away from the other eye. Do not let her rub it. Get medical help. Record it in the accident book.
Primer burn on the skin
Wipe off, rinse with plenty of water, and get medical help if the skin is red, sore or blistered.
Client feels dizzy, sick or has a headache
Stop, move her to fresh air, and check the extraction. Give water. Call for help if she does not recover.
Tingling, itching or burning in the fingertips during the service
Stop, clean product off the skin, and record it. Do not carry on. She may be reacting to the product.
Small fire
Switch off equipment, move away flammable bottles if it is safe, and use the Centre's extinguisher as you were trained. Raise the alarm.

ul: Store liquid monomer in its **closed, labelled** original bottle, in a cool, dry place out of direct sun and away from heat. Jamaica's heat can speed up evaporation and weaken the product.
Pour only a little into a small **dappen dish with a lid**. A big open dish gives off more vapour and picks up dust and powder.
Do not put used monomer back in the bottle: it is contaminated.
Left-over monomer in the dish at the end of the service is disposed of as the maker and the Centre say. Do not pour it down a sink or drain.
Wipes, cotton pads and paper towels with monomer on them go in a **metal bin with a lid**, emptied every day, away from heat and from the building's main exit.
Keep powder pots closed, so that they stay clean and dry.

blocks.note: Never mix or decant products into unlabelled bottles, or food and drink bottles. Someone could swallow the liquid or use it wrongly, and the directions and warnings are lost.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Hygiene and setting up the nail station

blocks.p: Nails and hands carry germs. A cut, a lifted enhancement or dirty tools can pass an infection from one client to the next. Good hygiene also stops germs getting under the acrylic, where they can grow in the warm, damp space and infect the nail.

head: Word
What it means
At the nail desk
rows: Cleaning
Removing dirt, dust and product with detergent and water. It always comes first, because disinfectant cannot work through dirt.
Scrubbing a cuticle pusher in warm, soapy water.
Disinfecting
Using a chemical at the maker's strength and for the full contact time to kill most harmful germs.
Soaking a clean metal pusher; wiping the desk.
Sterilising
Killing all germs, including spores, usually with an autoclave.
Used for some metal tools in other services.
Contact time
How long a surface or tool must stay wet with disinfectant.
Always the time on the label.
Single-use item
Used on one client only, then thrown away.
Orange sticks, paper files and buffers, tip applicators, disposable wipes.

blocks.note: A UV cabinet only keeps tools that are already clean and disinfected clean while they are stored. It does **not** disinfect dirty tools.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Item
After the client
rows: Wooden orange stick
Throw away
Paper or foam file, and buffer block
Throw away (or give to the client), because the surface cannot be disinfected
Metal cuticle pusher, nippers and tip cutters
Clean, then disinfect for the contact time, rinse if the label says so, dry and store covered. Metal tools may also be sterilised in an autoclave if the Centre has one.
Acrylic brush
Wipe, clean in monomer as the maker says, reshape the tip and store with the cap on, bristles up or flat
Dappen dish and dust brush
Clean and disinfect (dish); wash the dust brush
Towel
Fresh for each client; used ones into a closed laundry bin

blocks.h: Setting up before the client sits down

ul: Desk cleaned and disinfected; fresh towel and paper towel laid out.
Extraction on and working; light angled over the hands.
Everything within reach: tips, forms, files (100/180 and 180/240 grit), buffers, dehydrator, primer, cuticle oil, lint-free pads, powders, brushes and a small covered dish of monomer.
A lidded metal bin and a bowl of disinfectant ready.
Your own hands washed, nails short, no rings or bracelets that could scratch or trap product.

blocks.p: Setting up first means you never walk away from the client part-way through, and the acrylic does not set in the brush while you look for something.

Both you and the client wash your hands at the start, before any work on the nails. Then clean the nails with a nail-cleansing wipe or an antiseptic. Washing removes the dirt, oils and creams that make acrylic lift.

sections.title: Know the nail: structure, growth and conditions

head: Part
What it is
Why it matters for acrylic
rows: Nail plate
The hard, clear part you see, made of layers of keratin.
The surface the acrylic sticks to. Over-filing makes it thin and weak.
Nail bed
The skin under the plate; it has blood vessels and nerves.
Pink colour shows through. Damage here is painful and can harm growth.
Matrix
The root, under the skin at the base of the nail; the nail is made here.
Injury can cause ridges or permanent damage. Never push hard at the base.
Cuticle
A thin layer of dead skin on the nail plate, attached to the eponychium.
Must be gently pushed back and removed from the plate, or acrylic lifts.
Eponychium
The fold of living skin at the base of the nail.
A seal against germs. Do not cut it.
Side walls and nail grooves
The folds of skin along each side of the nail.
Keep product off them: a small gap prevents lifting and allergy.
Free edge
The part of the nail that grows past the end of the finger.
Where you add length, and where you cap and seal.
Hyponychium
The skin under the free edge that seals the nail bed.
Do not poke under it.
Lunula
The pale half-moon near the base.
Shows part of the matrix; no acrylic goes on the skin near it.

blocks.p: Fingernails grow about 3 mm a month (it varies), so a nail takes roughly four to six months to grow from the base to the free edge. New growth is why an enhancement needs an **infill** every few weeks.

blocks.h: The stress area, apex and C-curve

ul: The **stress area** is where the nail plate leaves the nail bed and the free edge begins. Most breaks happen here, because it carries the pressure when the nail is pushed or knocked.
The **apex** is the highest and strongest point of an acrylic nail. It sits over the stress area, so the thickest part of the product is where the nail needs the most strength.
The **C-curve** (or arch) is the curve across the nail. Look down the nail from the free edge: the curve should be even and the same on both sides.

blocks.p: A **contraindication** is something that means the service must not go ahead, or must be changed. A contagious (infectious) condition, one that can pass from person to person, stops the service. You are not a doctor: never name a disease to the client as a fact or try to treat it. Describe what you see, explain tactfully why the service cannot go ahead today, advise her to see a doctor, and record it.

head: Condition
What you see
What you do
rows: Paronychia (infection of the skin fold)
Red, swollen, painful, warm skin round the nail; may have pus.
Do not work on that nail. Refer to a doctor.
Onychomycosis (fungal infection of the nail)
Thick, yellow or brown, crumbling nail; may smell.
Do not apply acrylic: it traps germs and warmth. Refer to a doctor. Clean and disinfect everything you touched.
Onycholysis (nail plate separating from the nail bed)
White or yellow area where the nail has lifted; may follow injury, infection or a reaction.
Do not apply acrylic over it. Refer to a doctor if it is painful, infected or keeps happening.
Viral warts
Rough, raised growths on or near the nail.
Do not work on the area: they spread. Refer.
Nail bruise (blood under the nail)
Dark red, purple or black patch after a knock.
Do not apply over a recent bruise; a doctor should check it if it is large or painful.
Eczema, psoriasis or broken skin on the hands
Red, sore, cracked or scaly skin; cuts or grazes.
Avoid the area; do not work if the skin is broken or inflamed.
Earlier allergy to nail products
Red, itchy, swollen skin around the nails; nail lifting after previous sets.
Do not apply. Refer to a doctor. Record it.
Ridges, white spots, nail biting, thin or weak nails
Not infections.
Usually fine to go ahead; adapt, be gentle and do not over-file. Advise the client on care.
Diabetes, circulation problems
Poor healing, numb fingers.
Ask her to check with her doctor before the service.

blocks.note: Only one nail may be affected. You can still work on healthy nails, but clean and disinfect carefully and never touch healthy nails with tools used on the affected one. Check the Centre's rules.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.note: Heat, humidity and wet work are common in Jamaica, and fungal infections and paronychia are common in people whose hands are often wet. Ask about the client's work (dishwashing, cleaning, farming, laundry), because it affects how long a set will last.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: The consultation is a private conversation before the service. You find out what the client wants and whether her nails and health are fit for acrylic, agree a plan, and record it. Do it before you touch the nails, with the hands clean and in good light.

flow: Greet the client and ask her to wash her hands
Ask your questions
Look at the hands and nails in good light
Check for contraindications
Agree the look, length, method, time and price
Explain the aftercare and the infill
Complete the record card and get her signature

head: Ask about
Why it matters
rows: What she wants: length, shape, colour, pink and white or natural
Lets you choose tips or forms, and plan the products.
Health, medicines and skin conditions
Some conditions and medicines slow healing or affect the nails. Some need a doctor's approval.
Allergies, and any past reaction to nail products, gloves or cosmetics
To avoid a product that could cause a reaction. A past reaction to acrylic stops the service.
Her work and hobbies
Wet work, cleaning, farming, typing and sport affect how long the set will last and what shape suits.
Her own nail habits: biting, picking, using nails as tools
Biting damages the nail; using nails as tools breaks sets.
Previous enhancements and how they came off
Thin or damaged nails need extra care.
Whether she is pregnant or breastfeeding
Ensure good ventilation and follow the Centre's rules; keep exposure low.
Time and money
A full set takes time and needs an infill every 2 to 3 weeks. Tell her the price in JMD before you start.

head: Method
What it is
When you might choose it
rows: Acrylic overlay on natural nails
A thin acrylic layer over the client's own nail.
She has enough free edge and wants strength, not length.
Tips with an acrylic overlay
A plastic tip is glued on to give length and shape, then covered with acrylic.
She wants length; quicker and easier to shape; very short or bitten nails.
Sculpted acrylic on forms
A form is fitted under the free edge and the extension is built in acrylic, with no tip.
Very curved or unusually shaped nails where tips would not fit; pink and white; a custom shape.

ul: Date, name, contact details and age (a client under 18 needs a parent's or guardian's consent).
Health, medicines and allergies; any contraindication found and what you did.
Condition of the nails; the method, products and tip size used.
Her wishes, aftercare advice given, the date of her next infill, and the price in JMD.
Her **signature as consent**, and the date. Keep records locked away and private; under Jamaica's Data Protection Act they are personal information.

blocks.note: If the client has a contraindication, explain kindly and privately. Say what you have seen, never say what disease you think it is, and suggest she sees a doctor. Never discuss her nails or health with other clients.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: The acrylic system, products and tools

blocks.p: Acrylic is made by mixing a **liquid monomer** with a **powder polymer**. The monomer is made of small molecules. When it touches the powder, which holds a chemical that starts a reaction, the molecules join into long chains. This reaction is called **polymerisation**. It makes the hard, plastic-like nail. The mixed bead sets by this **chemical reaction on its own**: it needs no lamp and no activator spray.

ul: Warmth speeds the reaction. In a hot salon, on a hot day, or with warm hands, acrylic sets faster and you have less time to shape it. A cool room slows it down.
The product gives off a little warmth as it sets. Tell the client it may feel warm.
The powder may be clear, natural pink, cover pink or white, or coloured. Powders from different makers do not always match each maker's liquid: use the maker's system.

blocks.h: The mix ratio and the bead

blocks.p: The **mix ratio** is how much liquid there is compared with powder in a bead. The brush picks up liquid; you press it into the powder, and a ball of product (the **bead**) forms on the brush tip. The right ratio depends on the maker and the job, so follow the maker's instructions. As a rough guide, a good working bead holds its shape and has a wet shine, but does not run.

head: Bead
What it looks like
What goes wrong
rows: Too wet (too much liquid)
Very glossy, runny, flows towards the cuticle and side walls
It runs onto the skin and then lifts
It may shrink as it sets, be weak and discolour
It can cause skin irritation or allergy
Right consistency
Holds a rounded shape; slightly glossy; moves slowly when pressed
Easy to place and shape; strong when set
Too dry (too much powder)
Dull, crumbly or grainy; does not flow
Air bubbles, a rough surface and white or cloudy patches
Weak product that cracks and lifts

head: Item
What it is for
Take care
rows: Acrylic brush (often kolinsky sable hair)
Picks up liquid and powder; places and shapes the bead.
Wipe on a lint-free pad; clean in monomer; shape the tip; never leave it standing in liquid; cap it. Never use it for anything else.
Dappen dish
A small dish for the liquid monomer.
Small, covered, clean; use fresh monomer each client.
Powder pots
Clear, pink and white acrylic powder.
Keep closed and dry; do not dip the brush into the pot: take powder from a small separate dish if the maker says.
Nail tips and tip adhesive
Give length and shape.
Choose the right size for each nail; keep the adhesive off the skin.
Nail forms
A guide fitted under the free edge to sculpt length.
Snug, level and in line with the nail.
Primer
Helps acrylic stick to the natural nail.
Only a little, on the nail plate; never on the skin.
Dehydrator
Removes oil and moisture from the nail plate.
Apply only to the nail.
Files, buffers
Shape and smooth.
See the grit table. Single use.
Tip cutter, cuticle pusher, dust brush, lint-free pads, cuticle oil
Preparing, shaping and finishing.
Clean and disinfect or throw away as above.

blocks.p: The **grit number** tells you how coarse a file is. A **low number is coarse** (it takes product off fast), and a **high number is fine** (it smooths).

head: Grit
Used for
rows: Coarse: shortening and shaping hard enhancement only, never the natural nail
100/180 (a file with two grits)
Shaping the acrylic and shortening the free edge
Removing the shine from the natural nail lightly; refining the shape
240 and finer; buffer blocks
Smoothing and buffing the surface and the shine

blocks.note: Never use a coarse file on the natural nail. Even the fine file is used lightly: you are taking off only the shine, not the nail.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Most lifting begins with poor preparation. Acrylic sticks to a clean, dry, slightly roughened nail plate. It does not stick to oil, dust, water or cuticle.

flow: Wash hands, and remove any old polish with a non-acetone remover
Push the cuticle back gently with a pusher, and remove any dead skin from the nail plate
Shape the free edge and shorten it if needed
Remove the shine lightly with a fine file (180/240), without over-filing
Brush off the dust
Apply dehydrator to the nail plate only
Apply primer sparingly, to the nail plate only, if the maker's system uses one
Do not touch the prepared nails: oil from your skin or hers will cause lifting

head: Step
Why it matters
rows: Push back the cuticle and clear the plate
Cuticle left on the plate is a barrier: the acrylic sticks to it, and it lifts with it.
Remove the shine lightly
A smooth, glossy surface gives no grip. A rough surface grips. Over-filing thins the nail and makes it weak and sore.
Remove dust
Dust sits between the nail and the product and causes lifting.
Dehydrate
Removes oils and surface moisture so the product bonds.
Prime sparingly
A thin layer gives a chemical grip. Too much burns the skin, floods the cuticle and can cause allergy.

blocks.note: Cuticle oil and hand cream go on **after** the acrylic, not before. If the client has used hand cream or oil, wash her hands again and re-do the preparation.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.note: Humid weather and wet hands make a nail plate hold more moisture. Work in a dry, cool room if you can, and do not apply to nails that were in water just before.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Applying acrylic: tips, overlays and sculpting

flow: Choose a tip that fits the nail from side wall to side wall, without pinching or overlapping the skin
Check the tip's well (the shallow contact area) is not too deep; trim it if the maker says
Apply a thin line of adhesive to the well, never to the skin
Place the tip at the free edge at a slight angle, press it down towards the cuticle, and hold it for the time the maker says without air bubbles
Cut the tip to the length wanted
Blend the join (the 'well line') smooth with a fine file, taking care not to file the natural nail

ul: A tip that is too wide presses on the side walls and lifts; a tip that is too narrow leaves gaps that trap dirt.
A ridge left at the join shows through the acrylic and can lift. File only the tip, not the natural nail.
Air bubbles under the tip trap moisture and germs.

blocks.h: Applying the acrylic over a tip or natural nail

flow: Pour a little monomer into the covered dish and wipe the brush on a lint-free pad
Pick up the first bead with a good consistency
Place bead 1 at the free edge, then pat and press it back
Place bead 2 over the stress area to build the apex (the highest, strongest point)
Place bead 3 at the cuticle, thin, with a small gap from the skin and side walls
Smooth the acrylic into an even C-curve with the flat of the brush while it is workable
Let it set fully before you touch the surface with a file, and check it with the end of the brush handle: a hard 'click' means it has set

head: Area
How it should look
Why
rows: Free edge
Strong, even, a little thinner at the very tip
Gives the nail its length and shape without making it heavy.
Stress area (apex)
The thickest, highest point of the nail, in the middle of the nail
Takes the pressure and stops cracks.
Cuticle area
Very thin, smooth, with a small gap of about 1 mm from the skin
Thick product here lifts; product on skin causes lifting and allergy.
Side walls
Thin, straight and clear of the skin
Keeps the side walls free so that it can be cleaned and does not catch.
Whole nail
Even C-curve, the same on both sides; smooth, no bubbles or dips
Looks natural and wears well.

blocks.note: If acrylic touches the skin, wipe it away at once with a clean brush or a pad before it sets. If product has set on the skin, do not pick at it: file the product carefully, away from the skin, and tell your supervisor if the skin looks red or sore.
blocks.label: Tip

flow: Prepare the natural nail as before, and fit the form snugly under the free edge, in line with the nail, with no gaps at the sides
Check from the top and the side that the form is straight and the same on both sides
Place the first bead on the form for the free edge, shaped to the length wanted
Build the apex over the stress area with the second bead, and add a thin third bead at the cuticle
Let the acrylic set, then remove the form and shape the underside
File and refine the shape and the C-curve; buff and finish

ul: A loose form slides or leaves a gap, making the free edge thick or crooked.
A form fitted too low or at the wrong angle gives a nail that points up or droops.
Check that the form is fitted before you mix any product: acrylic will not wait.

blocks.p: A pink and white nail copies a natural look: white at the free edge, and pink over the nail bed.

ul: The **smile line** is the curved line where the white meets the pink. A good smile line is clear, even, and the same on every nail; a deep, even curve looks best on most nails.
Place the **white** bead first at the free edge on the form, shape the line neatly, and let it set slightly.
Place the **pink** over the nail bed, from the smile line to the cuticle, blending where they meet without smudging.
A dirty brush or a wet bead drags white into pink and ruins the smile line. Clean the brush between colours.

flow: Let the acrylic set fully
Shape the free edge and sides with a 100/180 file, working from the side walls to the centre
Smooth the surface and refine the C-curve with a finer file
Check the thickness at the cuticle: thin, with no ridge
Buff to a smooth shine
Brush off the dust and wipe the nails clean
Apply cuticle oil and rub it in
Apply polish if she wants it

ul: File **away from** the skin and the cuticle. Use light strokes and let the file do the work.
Extraction on, mask and glasses on, while you file.
A nail filed thin at the stress area breaks. Leave the apex strong.

head: Check from
Look for
rows: The top
Even length and shape on all nails; straight side walls; smooth, matching smile lines; no product on the skin
The side
Smooth, balanced curve; the apex over the stress area; thin at the cuticle; no hump or dip; no gap between tip and natural nail
The end (looking down from the free edge)
An even C-curve, the same on both sides; the edge not too thick
The surface
No bubbles, scratches, pits or cloudy patches; even shine
The client's comfort
No tightness, heat or pressure; the skin around the nails is calm

head: Advice
Why
rows: Wear gloves for washing up, laundry and cleaning, and avoid long soaks in water
Water and chemicals weaken the bond and the nail.
Do not use the nails as tools to open tins, scratch labels or pry things
Knocks break the apex or tear the nail.
Apply cuticle oil every day
Keeps the skin and the nail flexible and the cuticle neat.
Use a non-acetone remover to take off polish
Acetone dulls and softens acrylic.
Never pick, bite or pull a lifted nail; come back to the salon
Pulling takes layers of the natural nail with it.
Return for an infill every 2 to 3 weeks
The new growth shifts the balance and weakens the nail.
Report redness, itching, swelling, pain or colour change
These can be signs of infection or allergy.
Have the nails removed at the salon
Home removal tends to tear the natural nail.

head: Problem
Common causes
Prevention or action
rows: Lifting near the cuticle
Oil, dust or cuticle left on the nail
Bead too wet; product on skin
Product too thick at the cuticle
Thorough preparation; correct bead; thin and a small gap at the cuticle.
Lifting at the free edge or sides
Nail too thin or over-filed
Tip fitted badly or too wide
Wet work, knocks
Fit tips carefully, do not over-file, and advise on use.
Bubbles or cloudy patches
Bead too dry
Air trapped under the tip or in the product
Dirty brush
Correct the ratio; press the tip down and apply the bead smoothly.
Yellowing or discolouring
Old or contaminated liquid or powder
Smoking, dyes, strong cleaners, or UV (sun) over time
Use fresh product; keep pots closed and clean; advise the client.
Thick, lumpy or uneven surface
Bead too large or too dry
Product set before shaped
Work in smaller sections; file smooth.
Cracks across the nail
Apex missing or in the wrong place
Nail too thin at the stress area
Build the apex over the stress area.
Itching, redness, swelling
Allergy or irritation from product on the skin
Stop; remove product from the skin; refer; record.

blocks.note: Lifted acrylic is more than a looks problem. Water and germs can get under the gap and grow in the warm, damp space, causing a green-brown stain or an infection. Never fill over a lifted area: thin it away and rebuild.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: An **infill** (maintenance or rebalance) fills the grown-out gap near the cuticle and rebalances the nail so that the apex is back over the stress area. It is needed about every 2 to 3 weeks.

flow: Consult: ask about any problems, and check each nail for lifting, cracks, discolouration and infection
Remove any polish, then clean the hands
File the surface of the old acrylic to reduce the bulk, and thin and blend away any lifted product; never nip or pull it
Gently clear the cuticle and shape the free edge
Prepare only the new growth: remove shine from the regrowth, dehydrate, prime
Apply thin acrylic to the regrowth, with the apex rebuilt over the stress area, and blend it into the old product
File, shape, buff, check from all sides and apply cuticle oil
Give aftercare advice and rebook

blocks.p: Acrylic must never be prised, pulled or picked off. The product holds on to the top layers of the natural nail, so pulling it off takes those layers with it, leaving the nail thin, sore and open to infection.

flow: Work in a ventilated area, wear gloves, and keep acetone away from heat and flames
Cut the free edge short if it is long and file the bulk of the acrylic down, without touching the natural nail
Protect the skin round the nails with oil or barrier cream
Soak the nails in acetone, in a small dish or with acetone-soaked cotton wrapped in foil, for the time the maker says (often 15 to 30 minutes)
Gently ease the softened acrylic off with a wooden stick; if it will not move, soak it again rather than force it
Lightly buff any left-over product and the surface of the nail
Wash the hands, apply cuticle oil and hand cream, and advise the client to be gentle with her nails

ul: Acetone dries the skin and nails and its vapour can catch fire. Keep it away from heat and flames, keep the area ventilated, and keep skin protected.
Never rush a removal. Waiting costs less than a damaged nail.

blocks.note: Clients sometimes ask to keep their nails on for a special occasion that is weeks away. Tell her honestly how long a set lasts, and advise her to come back for an infill rather than leave the nails to lift. Lifted nails in the heat and damp are an infection risk.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: I can explain how acrylic is made and why it sets with no lamp.
I can control vapour and dust, and say why a dust mask and a desk fan are not enough.
I can explain why MMA must never be used, and how to spot a suspicious liquid.
I can name the correct gloves, store and dispose of monomer, primer and acetone safely, and give first aid for skin and eye contact.
I can explain cleaning, disinfecting and sterilising, and tell which tools are thrown away.
I can name the parts of the nail and say what the stress area, apex and C-curve are.
I can recognise paronychia, onychomycosis, onycholysis and warts, and say what to do.
I can carry out a consultation, complete the record card and get consent.
I can prepare the natural nail step by step and say why each step matters.
I can fit and blend tips, and apply an acrylic overlay with the apex over the stress area.
I can fit a form and sculpt a nail, including a pink and white smile line.
I can recognise a bead that is too wet or too dry, and say what goes wrong.
I can choose the right file grit for each job, and file safely.
I can check a finished nail from the top, side and end.
I can give aftercare advice, say when an infill is needed, and explain common faults.
I can carry out an infill and deal with lifting.
I can remove acrylic safely and explain why it must never be prised off.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each step, not only the step. For example: 'I remove the shine lightly so that the acrylic grips, but I do not over-file, because that thins the nail.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: The liquid part of acrylic. Professional liquid is EMA.
The chemical reaction in which monomer and polymer join and harden.
Ethyl methacrylate: the monomer used in professional nail liquid.
Methyl methacrylate: a liquid that must never be used on nails.
The maker's document on a product's hazards, first aid, storage and safe use.
A unit that draws vapour and dust away from the desk.
A small dish that holds the liquid monomer.
The amount of liquid compared with powder in a bead.
The ball of mixed acrylic picked up on the brush.
A product that helps acrylic stick to the natural nail; acid primer is corrosive.
A product that removes oil and moisture from the nail plate.
A number showing how coarse a file is; a low number is coarse.
The hard, visible part of the nail.
The skin under the nail plate.
The root of the nail, where it is made.
The fold of living skin at the base of the nail.
The dead skin on the nail plate, attached to the eponychium.
The folds of skin along each side of the nail.
The part of the nail that grows past the end of the finger.
The skin under the free edge that seals the nail bed.
Where the nail leaves the nail bed; most breaks happen here.
The highest, strongest point of an acrylic nail; it sits over the stress area.
The curve across the nail, seen from the free edge.
The curved line where the white meets the pink on a pink and white nail.
A plastic extension glued to the free edge to give length.
The shallow part of a tip that is glued to the natural nail.
A guide fitted under the free edge to sculpt acrylic length.
A layer of acrylic over a tip or natural nail.
Building the nail extension in acrylic on a form, with no tip.
Filling the grown-out gap at the cuticle and rebalancing the nail.
Anything that stops a service or means it must be changed.
A bacterial infection of the skin fold: red, swollen and painful.
A fungal infection of the nail.
The nail plate separating from the nail bed.
Becoming allergic through repeated skin contact with a product.
How long a surface must stay wet with disinfectant.

c1.title: Itchy fingers in Portmore
c1.text: Trudy-Ann Morgan, 29, comes to a salon in Portmore for a new set of acrylics. She says that after her last set at another salon, the skin around her nails became red, itchy and swollen, and two nails lifted. She has not had acrylics since. Trainee Shawna notes that the skin around the nails looks calm today and the nails look healthy. Trudy-Ann is keen to go ahead and says it was 'probably the heat'.

c2.title: A crowded desk in Half Way Tree
c2.text: In a small salon in Half Way Tree, Kevoy shares a room with a stylist. The door and windows are shut because the room is air-conditioned, and a small fan on the desk blows towards the client. He pours liquid monomer into a wide open bowl and leaves the bottle open beside it. A mosquito coil burns on the floor by the door, and used cotton pads soaked in monomer lie in an open plastic basket. His client, Mrs. Hibbert, says she has a headache.

c3.title: Lifting nails in Mandeville
c3.text: Trainee Kimberly applied acrylic over tips on a classmate in Mandeville. She pressed the bead into very little powder, so it looked glossy and ran towards the cuticle and onto the skin, and she worked quickly because the day was hot. After one week the acrylic has lifted at the cuticle on three nails. Kimberly also notes that the nails are thick at the cuticle and thin near the middle.

c4.title: Pink and white for a graduation in Savanna-la-Mar
c4.text: Shantel Brown wants pink and white nails for her graduation in Savanna-la-Mar. Her nails are short and very curved, and tips do not fit well. Trainee Odane plans to sculpt on forms. He fits the first form loosely, so there is a gap at one side. He places the white bead at the free edge, then pink over the nail bed, but his smile lines are uneven and there is white smudged into the pink.

c5.title: A set that is three weeks old in Ocho Rios
c5.text: Latoya, 31, works as a hotel housekeeper in Ocho Rios and has had a set of acrylic nails for three weeks. She has been picking at a nail that has lifted at the cuticle, and one nail has a green-brown stain under the lifted area. She asks the trainee, Rochelle, either to 'just pull them all off' or to fill them. Rochelle's instructor explains that the safe options are an infill or a soak-off removal.

questions.q: What should Shawna do about Trudy-Ann's earlier reaction?
o: Go ahead, because her skin looks calm and her nails look healthy today
Go ahead with a thinner bead and extra primer to keep product off the skin
Ask for details, record it, and not apply acrylic until a doctor has seen her
Use a different brand of powder, since powder is the usual cause of reactions
questions.why: A reaction after a previous acrylic set may mean sensitisation, which can last for life and can get worse. You cannot test for it at the desk, so you ask, record it, do not apply, and refer her to a doctor.

questions.q: Why is a reaction like Trudy-Ann's described as getting worse each time?
o: Each set thins the natural nail, so it soaks up more of the liquid
Skin contact with monomer builds up an allergy that can last for life
Salon extraction gets weaker with each visit, so more vapour reaches her
Primer left on the skin burns it a little more deeply each time
questions.why: Repeated skin contact with monomer can make the body sensitive (sensitisation). Once someone is sensitised, small amounts can set off the reaction again, so keeping product off the skin matters for every set.

questions.q: What should go on Trudy-Ann's record card?
o: Only the price and the date of the next infill
The earlier reaction, the decision made, and the advice given
Her nail shape and tip size, as the reaction is her own matter
The name of the salon that made the earlier set
questions.why: A full record of the history, the decision (not to treat, and why) and the advice given protects the client and the salon and tells the next technician what happened.

questions.q: What is the main fault in how Kevoy has set up ventilation?
o: The air conditioner makes the room too cold for the acrylic to set properly
The desk fan is too small to move enough air around the whole room
The monomer bottle is on the desk instead of in a closed cupboard
Shut windows and a fan blowing at the client keep vapour near her face
questions.why: A fan blowing across the desk pushes vapour towards the client's face, and sealed windows keep it in the room. Desk extraction that draws vapour away from both people, plus fresh air, is the control.

questions.q: What is the safest way to handle the monomer on Kevoy's desk?
o: Use a small covered dish and close the bottle after each use
Pour it into a larger bowl so the brush can reach all of it
Keep the bowl open so the vapour does not build up inside it
Pour left-over liquid back in the bottle so none is wasted
questions.why: A small, covered dish gives off less vapour and stays clean. Used monomer is contaminated and never goes back into the bottle.

questions.q: What is wrong with the pads and the mosquito coil?
o: Pads belong in a lidded metal bin, and no flame should burn near the desk
The pads should be kept in a cloth bag, and the coil moved to the other side of the door
The pads are fine in the basket if emptied weekly, but the coil should be kept in a metal dish
The pads should be sprayed with disinfectant, and the coil can stay by the door
questions.why: Monomer is flammable and its vapour can ignite, so used pads go in a lidded metal bin emptied daily, and nothing that burns or smokes belongs near the desk.

questions.q: Mrs. Hibbert says she has a headache. What should Kevoy do?
o: Give her water and carry on, but work faster to finish sooner
Stop, move her to fresh air, and fix the ventilation first
Tell her it is the air-conditioning and carry on with the set
Put a mask on her and carry on, since masks stop vapour
questions.why: Headache and dizziness are common signs of too much vapour. Stop, get her into fresh air, give water and correct the ventilation. A mask does not stop vapour.

questions.q: What is the main reason for the lifting at the cuticle on Kimberly's nails?
o: The tips were too long, so they pulled on the cuticle area as they grew out
The acrylic was left to set too long, so it shrank away from the skin
A bead that was too wet ran onto the skin and sat thick at the cuticle
The monomer was too cool to bond with the natural nail properly
questions.why: A wet bead floods onto the skin and the cuticle. Product on skin and thick product at the cuticle are both common causes of lifting. A thin application with a small gap prevents it.

questions.q: How should Kimberly have applied the product to prevent the thickness she found?
o: Free edge first, apex over the stress area, then a thin bead at the cuticle
Start with a large bead at the cuticle and work out towards the free edge
Build the apex at the cuticle and keep the free edge as thin as possible
Use one large bead in the middle and spread it over the whole nail
questions.why: Strength belongs at the stress area, in the middle of the nail, and the product should be thin at the cuticle and clear of the skin. Working in three controlled beads gives that shape.

questions.q: Kimberly worked quickly because the day was hot. What does heat do to acrylic?
o: It slows the reaction, so the acrylic stays soft for longer
It speeds up setting, so there is less time to shape it
It has no effect, because acrylic sets by itself in the same time
It makes the acrylic stronger, so it should be left to warm up
questions.why: Warmth speeds the chemical reaction, so acrylic sets faster in a hot room or with warm hands. Work in smaller sections so that you can shape each bead in time.

questions.q: What should Kimberly do about the lifted areas when the classmate returns for an infill?
o: Fill over the lifted areas so that the gap is no longer seen
Pull the lifted acrylic off by hand to see the nail underneath it
Leave the lifted nails alone and fill only the ones that are sound
Thin the lifted product away, prepare the nail and rebuild it
questions.why: Filling over lifting traps water and germs. The lifted acrylic is thinned and blended away with a file, never pulled, and the nail is prepared and rebuilt.

questions.q: What is the problem with Odane's loose form?
o: A form needs to be fitted only after the first bead has been applied
A loose form leaves a gap and makes the free edge thick or crooked
A loose form helps the acrylic to flow into the shape he wants
A form can be any size, as long as it is longer than the nail
questions.why: A form must fit snugly under the free edge and in line with the nail. A gap lets product run through and gives an uneven shape. Fit and check the form before you mix any product.

questions.q: Why would a sculpted nail suit Shantel better than a tip?
o: Sculpting needs no nail preparation, so it is quicker than fitting tips
A tip may not fit her very curved nails, but a form follows their shape
Tips cannot be used with pink and white, so a form is the only choice
Sculpted nails are lighter than tipped ones and so never need an infill
questions.why: A tip that does not fit a very curved nail pinches or leaves gaps. Sculpting builds the extension to the client's own nail shape, but it takes more skill and time.

questions.q: What should Odane do to fix the white smudged into the pink?
o: Use a wetter pink bead so the white blends in and the line softens
Put the pink on first and then paint the white over the top of it
Clean the brush between colours and place the white in a crisp line
File the smile line away and cover the whole nail with thick clear
questions.why: A clean brush and a controlled bead give a crisp smile line. A wet bead flows and drags colour; the smile line should be even and the same on every nail.

questions.q: When Odane checks the finished nails, which view best shows whether the C-curve is even?
o: From the top, looking straight down at the nail
Looking down from the free edge end towards the cuticle
From the side, at the apex
From the back of the hand, looking at all five nails together
questions.why: The C-curve is the curve across the nail, so you see it by looking down the nail from the free edge. The top view shows length and the smile line, and the side view shows the apex and thickness.

questions.q: What is the right advice for Latoya's request to pull the nails off?
o: Soak her hands in warm soapy water for an hour, then pull them off
Do not pull: thin the lifted areas for an infill, or file and soak off
Pull them off gently from the cuticle, as they are already loose
Cover the stained area with dark polish to stop water getting in
questions.why: Pulling takes layers of the natural nail with the product. The safe options are an infill (after thinning away lifted product) or a file-and-soak removal.

questions.q: What does the green-brown stain under the lifted area most likely mean?
o: Germs have grown under the lifted area, so it must be checked
It is a natural colour change in the nail that will fade by itself
It comes from too much primer left on the skin by the cuticle
It shows the acrylic is too thick at the free edge of the nail
questions.why: Water and germs can get under lifted acrylic and grow in the warm, damp space, causing staining or an infection. Remove the lifted product, check the nail, and refer if it looks infected.

questions.q: Latoya cleans hotel rooms all day. Which aftercare advice suits her best?
o: Soak her hands in warm water after work to keep the nails flexible
Use her nails to scrape stains off surfaces, since acrylic is hard
Wash her hands less often, so that the nails stay dry for longer
Wear gloves for cleaning and wet work, and oil her cuticles daily
questions.why: Water and cleaning chemicals weaken the bond and dry the nails. Gloves protect the set, and daily cuticle oil keeps the skin and nail flexible.

questions.q: A nail file is marked 100/180. What does this tell you?
o: It is a fine file for taking the shine off the natural nail
It is a buffer block for adding shine to the finished nail
One side is coarse (100) and one finer (180), for shaping acrylic
Both sides are very coarse, so it is used to take off old acrylic
questions.why: A low number is coarse and a high number is fine. A 100/180 file shapes hard product and shortens the free edge. Take the shine off the natural nail with a 180/240 file, used lightly.

questions.q: A trainee drips primer onto a client's skin by the side wall. What should she do?
o: Wipe it off and rinse the skin with plenty of water
Leave it, because the acrylic will cover it and seal it in
Cover it with acrylic quickly so it cannot reach the skin
Wipe it off with a dry pad only and carry on with the service
questions.why: Acid primer is corrosive and can burn the skin. Wipe it off straight away, rinse with plenty of water, and get medical help if the skin is red, sore or blistered. Record it.
